quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: You'll say this word every time you introduce yourself. At the start, do your lips close, or does your tongue tip lift?
quests.explanation: 'Name' starts with /n/ and ends with /m/. In 'My name is…', the first sound is the one listeners catch first. If your lips close at the start you get 'mame'. Use the tongue tip first, then close the lips at the end.
quests.mouthPosition: Touch your tongue tip to the ridge behind your upper teeth and hum through your nose, glide into 'ay', and close your lips for the final 'm'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: In 'the pleasure is mine', the middle of this word is voiced. Does your throat buzz there?
quests.explanation: 'Pleasure' has /ʒ/ in the middle: the tongue and lips take the same shape as for /ʃ/, but the voice buzzes through. Using /ʃ/ gives 'pleshure'. It's a polite word worth saying clearly.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'pleh', pull your tongue slightly back, round your lips, and blow air with your voice on before the weak 'er'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The spelling ends in CE. Does the ending hiss or buzz?
quests.explanation: 'Nice' ends in /s/: a voiceless hiss after a long vowel. Voicing it gives 'nize', which isn't a word. In 'nice to meet you', that crisp hiss closes the word.
quests.mouthPosition: Straight after the 'eye' glide, put the tongue tip near the ridge and blow a thin hiss with no voice.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: You'll use this word in every project meeting. At the very start, does the tongue tip tap with voice or with a puff?
quests.explanation: 'Deadline' begins with /d/, voiced. Devoicing gives 'tedline'. The word has a second /d/ after the first vowel and ends in /n/, so the buzz starts early and carries on.
quests.mouthPosition: Touch your tongue tip to the ridge with voice on, release softly into 'ed', then close for the second 'd' and press the tongue tip for 'l'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: This word ends with the letters GUE. Say the final sound: is it a voiced or a voiceless stop?
quests.explanation: 'Colleague' ends in /g/: the letters -gue are silent apart from the /g/ itself. Using /k/ gives 'colleek'. The word starts with a voiceless /k/ and ends with a voiced /g/.
quests.mouthPosition: After the long 'ee', lift the back of your tongue to the soft palate with voice on to close the word.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle is spelled G before E. Is there a closure before the buzz?
quests.explanation: 'Manager' has /dʒ/ in the middle: the tongue seals before releasing into a buzz. Using /ʒ/ gives 'manazher'. Saying 'my manager' clearly helps in work conversations.
quests.mouthPosition: On the third beat of the word, set the tongue front against the roof behind the ridge with voice humming, and give a quick buzzy release into the weak 'er'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle is spelled -ct-, but it sounds different. Is there a brief stop before the hush?
quests.explanation: 'Lecture' has /tʃ/ in the middle: /ˈlɛktʃər/. The /k/ is followed by a stop-then-hush, not a plain /ʃ/. Using /ʃ/ gives 'lecshur'. The -ture ending is /tʃər/ in many words, such as 'picture' and 'future'.
quests.mouthPosition: After the 'k', the front of the tongue touches the roof behind the ridge for a moment, then lets go into a voiceless hush before the weak 'er'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word is spelled with SS in the middle. Voiced or voiceless?
quests.explanation: 'Essay' has /s/ in the middle: SS spells a voiceless hiss. Voicing it gives 'ezzay'. The stress falls on the first syllable, so the /s/ closes it cleanly.
quests.mouthPosition: Once the stressed 'es' is said, keep your tongue tip near the ridge and hiss with no voice before 'ay'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE SECOND CONSONANT SOUND IN THE OPENING CLUSTER
quests.hint: After the back-of-tongue stop, does the tongue tip touch the ridge?
quests.explanation: 'Grammar' begins with /gr/. Using /l/ gives 'glammar'. The word has /m/ in the middle and a weak 'er' ending, so only the opening tongue shape needs care.
quests.mouthPosition: Lift the back of your tongue for the voiced 'g', keep it pulled back for 'r', and glide into 'am'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle consonant is voiced and sits between two short vowels. Which back-of-tongue sound is it?
quests.explanation: 'Luggage' has /g/ in the middle, followed by the ending /dʒ/. Using /k/ gives 'luckage'. At an airport counter, 'luggage' needs that voiced closure.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'lu-', lift the back of your tongue with voice on and release into the weak 'ij'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE SECOND CONSONANT SOUND IN THE OPENING CLUSTER
quests.hint: Say the first two sounds in slow motion. Which part of your tongue is busy for the second one?
quests.explanation: 'Flight' begins with /fl/: the hiss slides into /l/ with the tongue tip on the ridge. Using /r/ gives 'fright', a very different word. It matters at the check-in desk.
quests.mouthPosition: Rest your top teeth on your bottom lip and hiss, then press your tongue tip on the ridge for 'l' before 'ight'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The first sound is a seal and a release. Is your voice on?
quests.explanation: 'Journey' begins with /dʒ/: voiced. Using /tʃ/ gives 'churney'. The stressed vowel after it is r-coloured, so the voice needs to carry into it.
quests.mouthPosition: Seal your tongue behind the ridge with voice on, release into a buzzy hush, and glide into 'ur-nee'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: There's a silent letter near the end. Which sound actually closes the word?
quests.explanation: 'Receipt' ends in /t/; the P is silent. Saying the P gives 'receep-t'. At the checkout, 'receipt' needs only a clean tongue-tip stop.
quests.mouthPosition: Following the long 'ee', close the tongue tip against the ridge for a silent 't'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle has a hiss followed by a back-of-tongue stop. Voiced or voiceless?
quests.explanation: 'Discount' has /s/ before /k/: /ˈdɪskaʊnt/. Both are voiceless. Using /z/ gives 'diz-count'. Signs saying 'discount' are everywhere, and a clean hiss makes you easy to follow.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'dih', hiss with your tongue tip near the ridge and no voice, then close the back of the tongue for 'k'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The start is a lip closure. Is the release soft or puffed?
quests.explanation: 'Bargain' begins with /b/: lips close with voice on and release softly. Using /p/ gives 'pargain'. The stressed first syllable ends with an r-coloured vowel, so keep the opening voiced.
quests.mouthPosition: Close your lips with voice on, release gently into 'ar', and finish with 'gin'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: In 'turn left at the corner', the first sound is voiceless. Is there a puff at the very start?
quests.explanation: 'Corner' begins with /k/, with a puff of air. Voicing it gives 'gorner'. The word ends in an r-coloured vowel after /n/, so the opening consonant carries the clarity.
quests.mouthPosition: Lift the back of your tongue to the soft palate and release with a puff into 'or', then finish with 'ner'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle consonant is a lip-teeth sound. Voiced or voiceless?
quests.explanation: 'Traffic' has /f/ in the middle, spelled FF: /ˈtræfɪk/. Voicing it gives 'travic'. When you're reporting a delay, the voiceless hiss keeps the word clear.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'tra', rest your top teeth on your bottom lip and blow a voiceless stream of air, then finish with 'ik'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The ending is spelled -dge. Is the final sound voiced?
quests.explanation: 'Bridge' ends in /dʒ/, spelled -dge. The D is only part of the spelling. Using /tʃ/ gives 'britch'. In directions ('cross the bridge'), the voiced ending matters.
quests.mouthPosition: End by raising the tongue front to the roof behind the ridge, keep the voice going through a short closure, and open it into a brief buzz.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word begins and ends with consonants that look alike. At the start, is your voice on?
quests.explanation: 'Doctor' begins with /d/, voiced, and contains /k/ and /t/ later. Starting with /t/ gives 'toctor'. When booking an appointment, a clear opening matters.
quests.mouthPosition: Touch your tongue tip to the ridge with voice on, release into 'oc', then close for 'k' and 't'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: A weak syllable comes first. At the start of the stressed one, does your throat join in as the lip meets your teeth?
quests.explanation: 'Available' has /v/ at the start of the stressed syllable: /əˈveɪləbəl/. Using /w/ gives 'a-wailable'. Rounded lips instead of lip-teeth contact makes the word hard to recognise.
quests.mouthPosition: Raise your lower lip to your upper teeth as the stressed syllable begins, and let the voice buzz through the gap into 'vay'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: After the nasal, the lip-teeth sound starts the stressed syllable. Buzz or hiss?
quests.explanation: 'Confirm' has /f/ at the start of the stressed syllable: /kənˈfɜːrm/. Voicing it gives 'convirm'. When you confirm an appointment, the voiceless hiss keeps the word clear.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'kun', rest your top teeth on your bottom lip and hiss with no voice into 'firm'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle of the word is spelled SS. Voiced or voiceless?
quests.explanation: 'Password' has /s/ in the middle: /ˈpæswɜːrd/. Voicing it gives 'pazzword'. On tech-support calls, listeners need that crisp hiss.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'pa', hiss with your tongue tip near the ridge and no voice, then round your lips for 'w'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: In the middle, the lips close with voice on, just before a hiss. Voiced or voiceless?
quests.explanation: 'Website' has /b/ in the middle, followed by /s/. Devoicing gives 'wepsite'. Because the /b/ comes before a voiceless hiss, it's easy to let it go silent, but keep the buzz through the closure.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'weh', close your lips with voice on, then release straight into a hiss for 'site'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word ends with a voiced stop after a long vowel. Does the buzz last?
quests.explanation: 'Download' ends in /d/: voiced. Using /t/ gives 'downloat'. The first syllable also starts with /d/, so the word is built on two voiced stops.
quests.mouthPosition: Once the 'oh' is said, touch your tongue tip to the ridge with voice on and let it fade.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle consonant follows an r-coloured vowel. Does your lip touch your teeth?
quests.explanation: 'Service' has /v/ after the /r/ sound: /ˈsɜːrvɪs/. Using /w/ gives 'serwis'. On a customer call, 'service' is the word everyone listens for.
quests.mouthPosition: After the r-coloured vowel, your lower lip meets the upper teeth; keep the voice on so a soft buzz carries into 'vis'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: After the nasal, the lips close for a stop before the 'l'. Voiced or voiceless?
quests.explanation: 'Complaint' has /p/ after /m/ in /kəmˈpleɪnt/: voiceless. Using /b/ gives 'comblaint'. The lips are already closed for /m/, so only the voice needs to switch off.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'kum', keep your lips closed, switch off your voice, and release with a puff into 'play'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: After the weak first syllable, is the lip-teeth sound voiced?
quests.explanation: 'Refund' has /f/ in the middle: /ˈriːfʌnd/. Voicing it gives 'revund'. Requests for a refund need that lip-teeth hiss.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'ree', rest your top teeth on your bottom lip and hiss with no voice into 'und'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: At the start, hold your palm in front of your lips. Is there a puff?
quests.explanation: 'Party' begins with /p/: a puffed lip stop. Using /b/ gives 'barty'. A clear opening helps when you're inviting someone.
quests.mouthPosition: Seal both lips, then release with a clear puff into 'ar'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: After the nasal, there's a seal and a release. Is the release voiced?
quests.explanation: 'Enjoy' has /dʒ/ after /n/: /ɪnˈdʒɔɪ/. The affricate is voiced. Using /tʃ/ gives 'enchoy'. After a nasal, the voice carries on.
quests.mouthPosition: From the nasal, lift the front of the tongue to the roof behind the ridge in one move, voice humming, and let it open into a buzzy hush as you slide to 'oy'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: At the start, do your lips round, or does your lip touch your teeth?
quests.explanation: 'Weekend' begins with /w/: rounded lips. Using /v/ gives 'veekend'. The common question 'what are you doing this weekend?' depends on that first sound.
quests.mouthPosition: Round your lips tightly, spring them open into 'wee', and finish with 'kend'.
